questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has an 8 month history of mildly itchy red patches on her lower back, both knees and the backs of her elbows. They are coin-shaped, sharply demarcated and covered in thick silvery-white scale. She smokes 15 cigarettes a day. Her temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Well-demarcated, coin-shaped red plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces and the lower back are plaque psoriasis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: lower back, both knees and the backs of her elbows
steps.x: Extensor plaques, well demarcated, silvery scale.

elim: Eczema is poorly demarcated and flexural.
Discoid eczema is coin-shaped but crusted and weepy, not silvery.
Lichen planus has purple polygonal papules on the wrists.
Tinea is annular with central clearing.

steps.x: **D. Plaque psoriasis.** Plaque psoriasis: extensor surfaces, scalp, lower back.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has well-demarcated red plaques with silvery scale on both elbows. The dermatologist gently scrapes off the scale from one plaque with a glass slide to demonstrate a classic sign to medical students. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding?
o: Skin peels off with gentle lateral pressure
questions.e: Removing psoriatic scale reveals pinpoint bleeding (the Auspitz sign) from dilated dermal capillaries under thin suprapapillary epidermis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Scale removed from a psoriatic plaque.

elim: That is Nikolsky's sign in blistering disease.
White dermographism occurs in atopic skin.

steps.x: **B. Pinpoint bleeding points.** Auspitz sign: pinpoint bleeding on removing scale.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has a 1 year history of changes in several fingernails. There are many small pits in the nail plates, and the ends of two nails have lifted painlessly from the nail bed. He also has a scaly patch behind one ear and in his scalp. His temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Nail pitting and onycholysis with scalp plaques are classic psoriatic nail changes.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: small pits in the nail plates
lifted painlessly from the nail bed
steps.x: Pitting, onycholysis and scalp scale.

elim: Onychomycosis thickens and discolours nails without pits or scalp plaques.
Nail lichen planus causes ridging and nail loss.
Trauma does not pit several nails.

steps.x: **E. Psoriasis.** Psoriatic nails: pitting and onycholysis.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl has a 5 day history of many small, red, scaly, drop-shaped spots over her trunk and upper thighs. She has never had a skin problem before. Her temperature is 36.8°C. Her mother is asked about any recent illness.
questions.q: Which preceding event is most likely?
o: Contact with a new cat 2 days ago
questions.e: Guttate psoriasis is triggered by streptococcal infection, appearing 2 to 4 weeks later.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: never had a skin problem before
steps.x: Sudden drop-shaped scaly spots in a child.

elim: Varicella does not trigger guttate psoriasis.
Allergy does not cause this rash.
Too remote to be the trigger.

steps.x: **D. Sore throat 3 weeks ago.** Guttate: 2-4 weeks after streptococcal throat infection.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has a 1 week history of dozens of small, monomorphic, red, scaly papules over his trunk and arms. He had tonsillitis 3 weeks ago. There was no single large patch before the rash appeared. He is otherwise well, with temperature 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Monomorphic, drop-shaped scaly papules 2 to 4 weeks after streptococcal tonsillitis are guttate psoriasis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Drop lesions after strep throat, no herald patch.

elim: Pityriasis rosea starts with a herald patch and follows skin lines.
This causes hypo- or hyperpigmented macules, not drop papules.

steps.x: **A. Guttate psoriasis.** Guttate: post-streptococcal, drop-shaped, monomorphic.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with plaque psoriasis had a new tattoo on her forearm 3 weeks ago. Red, scaly, well-demarcated plaques have now developed exactly within the lines of the tattoo. There is no pus or pain. Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Allergic contact dermatitis to the ink
questions.e: New psoriatic lesions at sites of skin trauma are the Koebner phenomenon, from local activation of the same inflammatory pathways.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: exactly within the lines of the tattoo
steps.x: Psoriatic plaques along a site of skin trauma.

elim: Ink allergy is itchy and eczematous, not psoriatic plaques.
That is bleeding on removing scale.
There is no pus or pain.
That is skin shearing in blistering disease.

steps.x: **D. Koebner phenomenon.** Koebner: psoriasis at trauma sites.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with plaque psoriasis for 15 years has a 5 month history of pain and stiffness in his fingers. He has nail pitting and onycholysis on the affected fingers. His temperature is 36.8°C. Rheumatoid factor is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his hands?
o: Swelling of the distal interphalangeal joints
Swelling of the metacarpophalangeal joints with ulnar deviation
questions.e: Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis classically affecting the DIP joints, often with nail changes.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Psoriasis, nail disease, seronegative finger arthritis.

elim: Those are bony osteoarthritis nodes without inflammation.

steps.x: **B. Swelling of the distal interphalangeal joints.** Psoriatic arthritis: DIP joints.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has had severe plaque psoriasis for 20 years. He has a BMI of 34, waist circumference 108 cm and BP 148/92 mmHg. He asks which serious condition his psoriasis puts him at increased risk of. He does not smoke.
questions.q: Which condition is he most at risk of?
questions.e: Psoriasis is linked to metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease through shared chronic systemic inflammation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Severe psoriasis with metabolic features.

elim: Not a recognised complication of psoriasis itself.

steps.x: **B. Cardiovascular disease.** Complications: psoriatic arthritis, metabolic syndrome, CVD.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with mild plaque psoriasis has a 4 week history of a severe flare. Six weeks ago she was started on a new medication for performance anxiety and palpitations. She has no other medical problems and no recent infections. Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which medication is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Beta-blockers such as propranolol are classic triggers of psoriasis flares.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
New drug for anxiety with palpitations.

elim: SSRIs are not classic psoriasis triggers.

steps.x: **D. Propranolol.** Drug triggers: lithium, beta-blockers, aspirin, steroid withdrawal.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man with plaque psoriasis was given a 2 week course of oral prednisolone for a severe asthma attack. His skin cleared during the course. One week after stopping it suddenly, he has a widespread severe flare. His temperature is 37.0°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the flare?
questions.e: Stopping systemic corticosteroids is a recognised trigger for a severe psoriasis flare.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Flare after systemic steroid is stopped.
**D. Steroid withdrawal.** Steroid withdrawal triggers flares.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman has an atypical scaly plaque on her shin that has not responded to topical treatment. The dermatologist cannot be sure clinically whether it is psoriasis and takes a skin biopsy. Her temperature is 36.7°C. She has no lymphadenopathy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on biopsy if this is psoriasis?
questions.e: Rapid keratinocyte hyperproliferation causes incomplete maturation (parakeratosis) and a thickened epidermis, giving silvery scale.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Biopsy for an uncertain plaque.
**D. Parakeratosis with a thickened epidermis.** Psoriasis histology: parakeratosis and epidermal thickening.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has a 6 month history of an itchy scalp. There are thick, well-demarcated plaques of silvery scale in the scalp that extend just beyond the hairline onto his forehead and behind his ears. Hair growth is normal. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Thick, well-demarcated silvery plaques in the scalp extending beyond the hairline are scalp psoriasis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: thick, well-demarcated plaques of silvery scale
steps.x: Thick silvery scale beyond the hairline.

elim: Lice cause itch with nits, not plaques.
Seborrhoeic scale is greasy and yellow, not thick and silvery.
Tinea causes hair loss, mostly in children.

steps.x: **C. Scalp psoriasis.** Scalp is a classic psoriasis site.

questions.stem: A 15 year old boy is diagnosed with guttate psoriasis 3 weeks after a streptococcal sore throat. He has many small scaly drop lesions on his trunk. His mother asks what is most likely to happen. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely course of his rash?
o: It progresses to psoriatic arthritis within a year
It resolves within a few months
It spreads to his family members
questions.e: Guttate psoriasis usually resolves within months, so reassurance and emollient are first-line.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.
Guttate psoriasis natural history.
**D. It resolves within a few months.** Guttate usually resolves within months.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with plaque psoriasis had a transient ischaemic attack 6 weeks ago and was started on new medications. His psoriasis has since flared on his elbows and trunk. He has had no infections, injuries or alcohol excess. His temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which new medication is the most likely trigger?
questions.e: Aspirin is a recognised trigger for psoriasis flares, alongside lithium, beta-blockers and steroid withdrawal.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before you look at the options.

clues: no infections, injuries or alcohol excess
steps.x: New post-TIA drugs.

elim: Statins are not a recognised trigger.

steps.x: **A. Aspirin.** Triggers: lithium, beta-blockers, aspirin, steroid withdrawal.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has a single red, scaly plaque on the palm of her left hand for 9 months. It has not responded to a potent topical steroid. She has no other skin lesions and no nail changes. Her temperature is 36.8°C. Psoriasis, eczema and other causes are considered.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Psoriasis is usually a clinical diagnosis; a biopsy is only needed in atypical or uncertain cases like this single unresponsive palmar plaque.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.
Atypical solitary plaque.

elim: This is atypical, so it needs confirmation.
Not diagnostic of a skin lesion.
Patch testing is for contact allergy.

steps.x: **D. Skin biopsy.** Biopsy only in atypical/uncertain cases.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has plaque psoriasis on his trunk, legs and arms. The dermatology nurse estimates that 12% of his body surface area is affected (see item resources). Potent topical steroid with twice-daily vitamin D analogue has failed. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the best interpretation of his disease severity?
o: Moderate to severe; eligible for phototherapy
questions.e: Body surface area over 10% (or PASI over 10) defines moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, the threshold for escalating to phototherapy.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.
BSA over 10%, topicals failed.

elim: Biologics follow failure of phototherapy and systemic drugs.
Body surface area over 10% is enough.

steps.x: **B. Moderate to severe; eligible for phototherapy.** PASI >10 or BSA >10% = moderate-severe: phototherapy.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has plaque psoriasis on both elbows and knees. Her PASI score is 6 and about 4% of her body surface area is affected. Her plaques are improving on topical treatment. She asks if she needs light therapy. Her temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the best interpretation of her severity?
questions.e: Moderate to severe psoriasis is PASI over 10 or BSA over 10%; PASI 6 and BSA 4% are mild, so topical treatment continues.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.
Both measures below 10.

elim: Erythroderma affects over 90% of the skin.
She is far below the threshold.

steps.x: **B. Mild; topical treatment is appropriate.** Threshold: PASI >10 or BSA >10%.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man with plaque psoriasis is referred to dermatology. The consultant wants a standardised score combining the redness, thickness, scaling and area of his plaques in each body region to decide whether he is eligible for phototherapy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate assessment?
questions.e: PASI combines erythema, induration, scaling and area by body region; PASI over 10 defines moderate to severe disease.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the question being asked.
A severity score for psoriasis plaques.

elim: DLQI measures impact on life, not plaque severity.

steps.x: **C. Psoriasis Area and Severity Index.** PASI >10 = moderate-severe.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has newly diagnosed plaque psoriasis on her elbows, knees and lower back affecting about 2% of her body. She has had no treatment. She is not pregnant. Her temperature is 36.6°C and BP 116/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: First-line for plaque psoriasis is a potent topical corticosteroid plus a topical vitamin D analogue, both once daily (e.g. calcipotriol/betamethasone).

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Mild, untreated plaque psoriasis.

elim: Mild steroid is too weak for plaques.
Systemic therapy is for moderate to severe disease.

steps.x: **A. Calcipotriol and betamethasone once daily.** First-line: potent steroid + vitamin D analogue once daily.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has plaque psoriasis on his elbows and knees covering 4% of his body. He has used a potent topical corticosteroid and calcipotriol, each once daily, for 8 weeks. The plaques are only slightly better. His PASI score is 5. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase calcipotriol to twice daily with the steroid
questions.e: If once-daily steroid plus vitamin D analogue does not control psoriasis, increase the vitamin D analogue to twice daily with the steroid.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Mild disease, inadequate response to first-line.

elim: Biologics are for severe refractory disease.
Systemic therapy is for moderate to severe disease.
He is below the severity threshold.

steps.x: **A. Increase calcipotriol to twice daily with the steroid.** Next step: vitamin D analogue twice daily.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has scalp psoriasis with thick silvery scale through her hair. It is itchy and embarrassing. She has no plaques elsewhere and her nails are normal. She has had no treatment. Her temperature is 36.6°C and pulse rate 72 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Scalp psoriasis is treated with a potent topical corticosteroid such as betamethasone valerate.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Untreated scalp psoriasis.

elim: Mild steroid is too weak for scalp psoriasis.

steps.x: **A. Betamethasone valerate scalp application.** Scalp: potent topical steroid (betamethasone valerate).

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has scalp psoriasis that cleared after a 4 week course of betamethasone valerate scalp application. Two weeks later it has started to return and he wants to restart the steroid straight away. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Allow a 4 week break before another steroid course
Switch to a very potent steroid daily
Use the steroid twice daily for 3 months
questions.e: Courses of potent topical corticosteroids for scalp psoriasis should have a 4-week break between them.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Wanting a repeat steroid course too soon.

elim: Continuous potent steroid causes skin atrophy.
Systemic steroids worsen psoriasis on withdrawal.

steps.x: **A. Allow a 4 week break before another steroid course.** Scalp steroid courses: 4-week break between courses.

questions.stem: An 11 year old boy has a 2 week history of many small, red, scaly drop-shaped lesions on his trunk and limbs. He had a sore throat a month ago that settled. He is well and the rash is mildly itchy. His temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Potent topical steroid to every lesion
questions.e: Guttate psoriasis usually resolves within months; manage with reassurance and topical emollient.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Guttate psoriasis in a well child.

elim: Not needed for self-limiting guttate psoriasis.

steps.x: **E. Reassurance and topical emollient.** Guttate: reassurance and emollient.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis is about to start narrowband UVB phototherapy after topical treatment failed. He works outdoors as a gardener. He asks about the long-term risks of the treatment. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most important long-term risk to discuss?
questions.e: Narrowband UVB side effects include sunburn, skin ageing and increased skin cancer risk.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
UV light treatment.
**C. Increased risk of skin cancer.** NB-UVB: sunburn, skin ageing, skin cancer risk.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has a severe flare of plaque psoriasis covering 25% of her body. Topical treatment has failed. She is getting married in 4 weeks and needs rapid control. She may try for a baby next year. Her temperature is 36.7°C and BP 118/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Ciclosporin works quickly and is suitable for women of childbearing age.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: try for a baby next year
steps.x: Fast control in a woman planning pregnancy.

elim: Contraindicated in women who may become pregnant.
PUVA is for severe refractory disease and acts slowly.

steps.x: **C. Ciclosporin.** Ciclosporin: rapid, OK for childbearing age.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man has severe plaque psoriasis covering 20% of his body. It has not been controlled by topical treatment and a course of narrowband UVB. He has normal liver function and drinks no alcohol. He has no plans for children. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.e: Moderate to severe psoriasis that fails topicals and phototherapy is treated with systemic therapy such as methotrexate (an anti-folate).

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: normal liver function and drinks no alcohol
steps.x: Severe disease, topicals and phototherapy failed.

elim: Biologics come after failure of systemic therapy.
Systemic steroids risk severe flares on withdrawal.

steps.x: **C. Methotrexate.** Systemic: methotrexate, or ciclosporin/acitretin.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has severe plaque psoriasis. The dermatologist is choosing a systemic drug. Topicals and narrowband UVB have failed. She is planning to start a family within the next 2 years. Her temperature is 36.7°C and BP 114/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which drug is contraindicated?
questions.e: Acitretin, an oral retinoid, is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women who may become pregnant.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: start a family within the next 2 years
steps.x: Systemic drug choice in a woman planning pregnancy.

elim: Ciclosporin is suitable for women of childbearing age.

steps.x: **A. Acitretin.** Acitretin: contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man started a systemic drug for severe psoriasis 3 months ago. He now has dry, cracked lips, dry eyes, thinning hair and low mood. His liver enzymes are mildly raised. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Acitretin causes dry mucous membranes, hair thinning, hepatitis, depression and suicidal ideation.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Mucosal dryness, hair loss, mood change, liver.

elim: Biologics cause infection risk, not these effects.
Phototherapy causes sunburn and skin ageing.

steps.x: **A. Acitretin.** Acitretin: dry mucosa, hair thinning, hepatitis, depression.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has severe plaque psoriasis covering 30% of his body. It has failed topical treatment, narrowband UVB, methotrexate and ciclosporin. He has no history of tuberculosis or malignancy. His PASI score is 22. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
o: Repeat methotrexate at the same dose
questions.e: Severe psoriasis refractory to systemic therapy is treated with biologics such as adalimumab or ustekinumab.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: failed topical treatment, narrowband UVB, methotrexate and ciclosporin
steps.x: Severe, refractory to systemic therapy.

elim: Weak, and does not address refractory disease.

steps.x: **B. Biological therapy such as adalimumab.** Refractory: biologics (adalimumab, ustekinumab).

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with severe psoriasis is offered PUVA photochemotherapy after other treatments failed. He has fair skin and had several sunburns as a child. He asks about the main cancer risk. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which cancer risk is most increased by PUVA?
questions.e: PUVA photochemotherapy is used for severe psoriasis but increases the risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.
Psoralen plus UVA.
**E. Squamous cell carcinoma.** PUVA: increased SCC risk.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has chronic stable plaque psoriasis on her elbows and knees. A potent steroid and vitamin D combination cleared the flare. She wants a treatment she can keep using long term without the risk of skin thinning. Her temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term treatment?
questions.e: Calcipotriol, a topical vitamin D analogue, can be used long term without steroid skin thinning.

steps.x: A management question: decide what the next step is for this patient now.

clues: without the risk of skin thinning
steps.x: Long-term, steroid-sparing topical.

elim: Very potent steroid continuously causes atrophy.
Too toxic for long-term mild disease.

steps.x: **B. Calcipotriol.** Long term: calcipotriol.

questions.stem: A medical student examines a skin biopsy from a 42 year old man with plaque psoriasis. The pathologist explains that keratinocytes in his plaques move from the basal layer to the surface far faster than in normal skin, which takes about 28 days.
questions.q: Approximately how long does keratinocyte turnover take in a psoriatic plaque?
questions.e: In psoriasis keratinocyte turnover shortens from about 28 days to as little as 3 to 5 days.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.

clues: far faster than in normal skin
steps.x: Accelerated keratinocyte cycle.
**D. 3–5 days.** Turnover: 28 days normally, 3-5 days in psoriasis.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has plaque psoriasis. Her dermatologist explains that her plaques are driven by an immune process that accelerates the keratinocyte cell cycle, and that her new injection targets this pathway. Her temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which immune pathway drives psoriatic plaques?
questions.e: Psoriasis is a T-cell mediated process driven by the Th17/IL-23 axis, accelerating keratinocyte turnover.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.
T-cell pathway in psoriasis.
**D. Th17/IL-23 axis.** Psoriasis: Th17/IL-23. Eczema: Th2.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has had well-demarcated, silvery-scaled plaques on his knees and elbows for 5 years. When the scale is removed, small bleeding points appear. A student asks which microscopic changes underlie this sign. His temperature is 36.6°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Fragile blood vessels from vitamin C deficiency
Thin epidermis over dilated dermal capillaries
questions.e: The Auspitz sign reflects thinning of the suprapapillary epidermis over dilated, tortuous dermal capillaries.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.
The Auspitz sign.

elim: Bleeding is local, not from thrombocytopenia.

steps.x: **C. Thin epidermis over dilated dermal capillaries.** Auspitz: thin suprapapillary epidermis over dilated capillaries.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man with severe plaque psoriasis starts ustekinumab injections after methotrexate and adalimumab fail. His plaques clear over 16 weeks and his PASI falls from 24 to 2. A student asks which cytokines the drug blocks. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which cytokines are blocked by ustekinumab?
questions.e: Ustekinumab targets the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23, blocking the Th17 inflammatory pathway.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.
Mechanism of ustekinumab.

elim: Those are targeted by other drugs.
Those are Th2 cytokines targeted in eczema.

steps.x: **B. IL-12 and IL-23.** Ustekinumab: anti-p40, blocks IL-12 and IL-23.

questions.stem: A 13 year old girl develops guttate psoriasis 3 weeks after group A streptococcal tonsillitis. She has no previous skin disease and cultures of the skin lesions are sterile. Her mother asks why a throat infection caused a skin rash. Her temperature is 36.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Bacterial spread through the blood to the skin
Molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and keratinocyte proteins
questions.e: Guttate psoriasis is thought to result from molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and keratinocyte proteins, triggering an acute T-cell response.

steps.x: A science question: link the finding to the mechanism behind it.

clues: 3 weeks after group A streptococcal tonsillitis
why a throat infection caused a skin rash
steps.x: Post-streptococcal skin disease.

elim: That is scarlet fever or SSSS.

steps.x: **C. Molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and keratinocyte proteins.** Guttate: molecular mimicry.
